model.description: Partial reconstruction of Level-0 definitions and scoped physical, chemical, biochemical, cellular, optical, retinal, visual and neural evidence. Levels organize the display; they do not establish a universal emergence order. Formal specifications, computational models, experimental preparations, observations and conditional interpretations have distinct roles. Each scientific claim retains its reviewed sources, selected system, observable, uncertainty, shared inputs and unresolved limitations. Field and particle models remain distinct from detector response, lattice calculations and conditional parameter extraction. Nuclear and atomic masses, primordial abundances and cosmological spectra retain their source-specific calibration, model and covariance limits. Atomic and molecular binding, prepared-state spectroscopy, charge production, electrolyte screening and stationary electronic representations address different questions; their energy comparisons do not by themselves establish formation kinetics, universal stability or a unique ancestry. Optical and neural records distinguish measured response from anatomy, intervention and theoretical interpretation. Cellular organization, state regulation, fate and immune responses retain preparation-specific perturbations, finite persistence, partial rescue, contrary outcomes and corrected controls. Model-derived metabolic flux and inferred immune networks remain distinct from measured readouts. Behavioral success and fitted models do not identify a unique mechanism. Finite checks reproduce only their declared data or mathematical witnesses, not entire experiments. Cross-domain construction, universal parent weights and carrier minima, downward causation and a derivation of quantum theory from Level 0 remain unestablished. Source discrepancies and unreproduced stages remain explicit. No whole-graph scientific validation is claimed.
model.name: Causal Emergence — Canonical Reconstruction

nodes.name: Test a persistent ensemble
nodes.shortDescription: carrier closure; collective persistence; comparison with uncoupled and alternative couplings; defined collective observables

nodes.name: Admit a mode candidate
nodes.shortDescription: consistent operator and dispersion convention; specified domain, units and boundary conditions; stationarity residual and convergence within declared tolerances

nodes.name: Test localized objecthood
nodes.shortDescription: declared independent variables and equations; localization under domain enlargement; nontrivial concentration; stationarity; specified static and dynamic perturbative persistence

nodes.name: Test a new carrier interface
nodes.shortDescription: explicit forward abstraction map; declared state and intervention domain; macro closure error and uncertainty; substitution/interface test; independent target or analytical certificate

nodes.name: Compare eligible candidates
nodes.shortDescription: fully specified functional; eligible candidate cohort; frozen coefficient and tolerance policy; retain all tied extrema; sensitivity analysis

nodes.name: Test joint triadic closure
nodes.shortDescription: admitted modes; signed frequency and wave-number balance; declared simple-cycle and rank surrogate; removal witnesses for the exact closure predicate

nodes.name: Finite activated-helper rate effect
nodes.shortDescription: For the selected downstream-helper comparison, the source reports that activated AGC increases single-G primer-extension rate by more than two orders of magnitude relative to its unactivated helper variants. Product-length gels and primer-loss fits support a finite helper-dependent nonenzymatic extension effect, while the microscopic catalytic mechanism remains conditional.

nodes.name: Activated nucleotide substrate and energy-supply boundary
nodes.shortDescription: The source reports prepared activated RNA species and helper-dependent extension;the existing Mansy context supplies a different externally provided activated amino-nucleotide in a vesicle assay. These retain concrete activation chemistry and reactive substrates without deriving a universal chemical energy,prebiotic supply route or self-renewing biochemical organization.

nodes.name: Activation Gibbs energy in elementary transition-state theory
nodes.shortDescription: Activation Gibbs energy and its rate relation under the stated elementary-rate and standard-state convention.

nodes.name: Scoped allosteric binding and amide-exchange modulation
nodes.shortDescription: Card3.33 is qualified to ligand-dependent binding-preference inference and local amide-exchange protection in CAPN. These readouts show finite local chemical/interaction response without measuring intrinsic bond strength, electronic interaction potential, catalytic competence or a general global-to-local chemical law.

nodes.name: Distal allostery and local chemical-readout boundary
nodes.shortDescription: Use allostery here for a declared distal response to ligand binding in the same connected CAPN assembly, while keeping the measured response separate from the communication mechanism. The source binding affinity, chemical shift, relaxation and amide-exchange readouts differ. A change in exchange protection is not an intrinsic bond-dissociation energy, electronic interaction potential, catalytic turnover or proof that every allosteric response requires a large mean conformational change.

nodes.name: Source-fitted alpha-lytic protease folding/unfolding rates
nodes.shortDescription: At 4 C the source reports a very small initial I-to-N rate kf=(1.18 +/- 0.06)e-11 per second and a zero-guanidinium unfolding extrapolation ku=(1.8 +/- 0.2)e-8 per second. It reports Pro-dependent fast-phase saturation at 0.037 +/- 0.004 per second in its separate catalyzed protocol. These are activity-calibrated initial-rate and spectroscopy-fit quantities; the corresponding millennial folding half-times are extrapolated, not directly timed incubations.

nodes.name: Conditional alpha-lytic protease kinetic-metastability inference
nodes.shortDescription: Using its rate ratio for the I/N reaction, Sohl and colleagues infer that I is favored over native N by 4.0 +/- 0.1 kcal/mol at 4 C and 5.9 +/- 0.5 kcal/mol at 25 C. Their interpretation is an active native state persisting behind a large kinetic barrier rather than being the minimum-free-energy I/N state. This is a preparation- and model-dependent counterexample to treating functional folded persistence as universal thermodynamic ground-state occupancy.

nodes.name: HEWL-D1.3 crystallographic context
nodes.shortDescription: The source measures X-ray diffraction from a complex of hen egg-white lysozyme and murine monoclonal D1.3 Fab, crystallized in 15-20 percent PEG8000 at pH6.0, monoclinic P21 with one complex per asymmetric unit. Data extend to 2.8 angstrom. Isomorphous/anomalous phases and density modification precede restrained least-squares refinement and omitted-segment model checks. The current R factor is0.28 over20-2.8 angstrom, with approximate coordinate error0.6 angstrom; no solvent molecules were located. Antibody sequence and comparison native-lysozyme coordinates are adopted from cited/personal-communication inputs. Crystal temperature, full solution concentrations and a direct unbound D1.3 control are not supplied in the reviewed article.

nodes.name: Prepared RNase chemical refolding context
nodes.shortDescription: Reduce bovine pancreatic RNase with mercaptoethanol in 8 M urea; remove reagents by Sephadex G25. Adjust the resulting reduced-chain preparation to pH 8.2 with tris-acetate and oxidize in open beakers at 23-24 C at 2.0 or 0.1 mg/ml. Follow SH disappearance by p-chloromercuribenzoate and radiolabeled iodoacetate, optical rotation at 366 nm and UV spectra. Acidified aliquots are assayed at pH 5 against RNA and separately uridylic-2-prime,3-prime-cyclic phosphate with native-enzyme controls.

nodes.name: Antibody interface versus binding-mechanism boundary
nodes.shortDescription: For this review, a refined antigen-Fab interface provides a structural example of associated protein recognition. Static contacts and geometric complementarity differ from an affinity constant, specificity panel, association/dissociation kinetics, conformational-adjustment route and downstream immune response. None is inferred solely from the bound crystal.

nodes.name: Finite antigen-antibody recognition source scope
nodes.shortDescription: Resolve original card 3.11 to the actual source bound HEWL-D1.3 interface and its crystallographic uncertainty. Structural association, discontinuous epitope geometry and assigned noncovalent-contact patterns are admitted; quantitative specificity/affinity, adaptive binding route, induced-fit/selection/lock-and-key conclusions and downstream immune function remain outside admission.

nodes.name: Purified DM-MBP refolding and aggregation context
nodes.shortDescription: Use purified mature DM-MBP V8G/Y283D, normally100 nM at 25 C, plus concentration-series and wild-type controls. The chloride-containing arm dilutes100-fold from 6 M guanidine-HCl into 20 mM Tris-HCl pH7.5,200 mM KCl and 5 mM Mg(OAc)2. The chloride-deficient arm dilutes100-fold from 9.5 M urea into 100 mM Hepes pH7.5,20 mM KOAc and 5 mM Mg(OAc)2. In each chaperonin arm capture with 250 nM GroEL or SR1, then add 250 nM GroES and 5 mM ATP. Record tryptophan fluorescence at 295 nm excitation/345 nm emission and separate dynamic light scattering. The two solution protocols differ in several components.

nodes.name: Purified Rubisco chaperonin refolding context
nodes.shortDescription: Use purified R. rubrum Rubisco at 80 nM and 15 C. Dilute100-fold from 5 M guanidine-HCl,100 mM Tris-HCl pH7.5,1 mM EDTA and 20 mM DTT into 50 mM Tris-HCl pH7.7,10 mM KCl,7 mM MgCl2 and 2 mM DTT, with or without 7.5 micromolar BSA. For chaperonin arms include 2 micromolar GroEL or SR1 during capture, then add 2.5 micromolar GroES and 5 mM ATP. Quench timed aliquots with hexokinase/glucose and assay radiochemical Rubisco activity. SR1 aliquots receive4 C for 10 min to release GroES and permit dimerization. Separately monitor dynamic light scattering and Superose6 elution of 35S-labeled Rubisco in the solution-plus-BSA reaction, with native/BSA controls.

nodes.name: Catalytic closure and resource boundary
nodes.shortDescription: For this finite case, distinguish reciprocal ligation-based production of two RNA catalysts from synthesis of all substrates/resources, arbitrary genome copying, protein enzyme ancestry, formal RAF/food-generated closure and indefinite autonomous persistence. Observed externally replenished amplification does not establish all of those broader properties.

nodes.name: Finite cross-catalytic network scope
nodes.shortDescription: Card 3.13 is qualified to a defined protein-free pair of mutually catalytic RNA ligation reactions with observed substrate-dependent batch/serial amplification. The source supports a finite prepared network organization; formal RAF generality, historical early-life stage, unrestricted component self-production, universal protein/cooperativity prerequisites and indefinite autonomous persistence are outside admission.

nodes.name: Biochemical electron-capture modulation: unsupported hypothesis
nodes.shortDescription: Biochemical or enzymatic modulation of a specified electron-capture channel remains an unsupported hypothesis within this review. The existing isotope-specific Pr140 storage-ring result establishes an electronic-state dependence in highly stripped ions; it does not establish the biochemical intervention asserted by original card 3.37. The draft empirical extension is excluded from the admitted findings without claiming that all biochemical electron-capture effects are absent.

nodes.name: Boundary for transferring electronic-state decay evidence to biochemistry
nodes.shortDescription: A biochemical electron-capture claim requires a specified isotope and nuclear channel, a specified biochemical/electronic preparation, a matched comparison and a rate readout with its loss, background and uncertainty model. Evidence from highly stripped ions constrains electronic-state dependence in that preparation; it does not by itself supply a biochemical intervention.

nodes.name: Prepared hammerhead ion-series cleavage and controls
nodes.shortDescription: Prepare purified transcribed hammerhead/substrate RNA, reduce trace metals by EDTA treatment/buffer exchange and Chelex, and anneal a 10:1 ribozyme:substrate mixture with 0.5-1 micromolar final ribozyme. At 25 C compare1 mM divalent-metal additions in 50 mM Tris pH 7.0, 0.1 M NaCl and 0.1 mM EDTA; measure fast reactions with 2 ms-dead-time quench flow and slower reactions manually. Quantify PAGE bands and fit an approach-to-equilibrium progress curve. Retain the separate 2 M NaCl, pH/metal extrapolation and slow-population/pulse-chase tests.

nodes.name: Prepared hammerhead I-II FRET and ion controls
nodes.shortDescription: Anneal chemically synthesized Cy3-labelled hammerhead and Cy5-labelled deoxy-substrate strands, including a UUCG-loop control. Dilute to about 25 nM in 50 mM Tris, pH 7.0, 100 mM NaCl and 0.1 mM EDTA; at 25 C titrate Ca, Mg, Mn, Sr or specified monovalent ions. Use IA/(IA+ID) from 500 nm excitation and 560/660 nm emission, with dilution and source Mn-quenching corrections, to fit a phenomenological metal-dependent response.

nodes.name: Similar global folding responses despite different ion identities
nodes.shortDescription: Boots Table 2 reports wild-type global-FRET metal midpoints in mM: Mn 0.87±0.5, Mg 1.2±0.2, Ca 1.4±0.2 and Sr 2.0±0.2; corresponding Hill coefficients 0.41, 0.56, 0.57 and 0.65. The UUCG-loop control requires midpoints 5.2, 6.2, 9.0 and 12 mM. These comparable global stem-proximity responses across the four ions contrast with the much larger variation in the separate cleavable-RNA apparent rates. At 1 mM Mg the noncleavable FRET response changes by less than 3% over 8 h even while a separate cleavable preparation slowly increases its product fraction.

nodes.name: Metal-dependent apparent hammerhead reaction rates
nodes.shortDescription: In 0.1 M NaCl at 25 C, pH 7.0 and 1 mM added metal, Boots Table 1 reports apparent kobs values in min^-1 of Mn 200±10, Co 140±20, Zn 82±9, Cd 72±5, Mg 2.6±0.3, Ca 0.14±0.04 and Sr 0.018±0.006. The source defines this response as cleavage-plus-ligation equilibration of the rapidly reacting fraction. In a separate 1 mM Mg slow-population experiment, the cleaved fraction increases from about 0.30 to 0.65 over 8 h with fitted 0.003 min^-1; a different noncleavable FRET preparation remains nearly unchanged globally.

nodes.name: Conditional heterogeneous BPTI hydration dynamics
nodes.shortDescription: The source interprets its supercooled MRD through a small strongly retarded water subpopulation plus a more mobile majority. At-30 C, assigning the low-frequency component to external surface sites gives source residence times about 10-15 ns and an order-weighted amplitude consistent with roughly three or more waters, not an exact count. The residual factor about 2 constrains broadly immobilized hydration for this model/preparation. Surface/internal assignments, the more-than 95 percent interpretation and extrapolation to ordinary temperature remain conditional, especially given SI S7 W111 inconsistency; no universal long-range ordered shell follows.

nodes.name: Source-fitted BPTI MRD parameters
nodes.shortDescription: With the highest-frequency point excluded, Table 5 reports apparent beta correlation times10.7±0.7 ns for 2H and 8.9±0.9 ns for 17O at-10 C, and 11±1 ns for 2H at-30 C. Apparent Nbeta*Sbeta^2 values are1.7±0.1,1.2±0.2 and 3.3±0.4, respectively. With an adopted surface-water number268, source-derived residual rotational retardation factors are3.3±0.2,3.8±0.2 and 2.1±0.2. These are conditional source fits and derived quantities, with reported68.3 percent uncertainties, not direct site counts or independently reproduced rates.

nodes.name: BPTI water relaxation dispersion
nodes.shortDescription: The source records water 2H and 17O longitudinal-relaxation frequency dependence for the BPTI emulsion at-10 C and 2H at-30 C, with same-condition bulk-water baselines. Figure 4 shows a low-frequency excess that decreases across the measured frequency range and a residual high-frequency excess. These are aggregate water-nuclear relaxation observations, not separately imaged hydration layers or ion positions.

nodes.name: Ligand-dependent CAPN amide H/D exchange protection
nodes.shortDescription: The source measures amide-proton exchange from HSQC intensity time courses under identical exchange conditions for the three assigned ligation states. The first cAMP comparison gives limited protection largely in the liganded subunit; the second gives a broader decrease in exchange rates, particularly around the dimer interface. This is a finite ligand-dependent change in local exchange/protection, rather than direct measurement of stronger individual covalent or hydrogen bonds.

nodes.name: Ligand-dependent distal CAPN relaxation response
nodes.shortDescription: Relative to apo CAPN, the nominal singly liganded preparation shows increased slow-exchange contributions in both subunits, including remote residues mapped up to about35angstrom from bound cAMP in the adopted structural model. Adding the second ligand suppresses the measured slow/fast-motion signatures more widely. The unliganded pocket has small mean chemical-shift perturbations in the first-step comparison, so the source supports a distal dynamic response without resolving a unique communication pathway.

nodes.name: Conditional CAPN conformational-entropy interpretation
nodes.shortDescription: The source combines ITC total thermodynamics with NMR motion changes to interpret the negative cooperativity as dynamics-mediated. Its backbone-order-parameter model estimates first/second conformational penalties -T*deltaSconf=3.2 and18.1kcal/mol. These are upper-bound model estimates under uncorrelated-motion assumptions; their difference is not the same quantity as the about4kcal/mol total entropy difference from ITC. The data support a conditional dynamic/entropic account, not exclusive identification of an entropy-only microscopic mechanism.

nodes.name: Prepared CAPN ligation-state comparison
nodes.shortDescription: The controlled series changes supplied cAMP while retaining the source CAPN construct and NMR protocol. Apo and doubly liganded preparations show one principal set of subunit signals, whereas the nominal singly liganded preparation shows distinct liganded/unliganded signal sets. These are the source occupancy assignments used to compare local and remote responses, without a newly asserted100-percent pure state population.

nodes.name: Source-fitted CAPN sequential binding and thermodynamics
nodes.shortDescription: The biphasic CAPN ITC isotherm is fitted with a sequential-site model. Figure7 reports first/second step Kd=0.04 and4micromolar and corresponding rounded deltaG=-10.3 and-7.5kcal/mol. It reports deltaH=-1.8 and-2.9kcal/mol and total -T*deltaS=-8.5 and-4.6kcal/mol. Thus the second step is less favorable overall in the source interpretation despite a more favorable enthalpy; its relative total entropic penalty is about4kcal/mol. This is negative cooperativity, not sensitivity amplification inferred from a positive Hill slope.

nodes.name: Catalytic rate changes and the equilibrium boundary
nodes.shortDescription: The definitional boundary between catalytic rate changes and the net reaction equilibrium at fixed conditions.

nodes.name: Finite supplied CETCH cyclic operation
nodes.shortDescription: The joint isotope-label/product evidence supports recurrent carbon-fixation operation in the supplied CETCH 5.4 network over the measured 90-minute interval. This goes beyond isolated stepwise conversion, which had not assured operation of CETCH 1.0, but remains a conditional source interpretation of finite cyclic flux rather than autonomous catalyst synthesis, complete mass balance, global steady state or adaptive regulation.

nodes.name: CETCH labeling and coupled output
nodes.shortDescription: For source CETCH 5.4, six intermediate abundance/isotopologue time courses become progressively labeled over 90 minutes while the coupled trap yields source-reported 540 micromolar malate. The authors assign this to 1080 micromolar fixed CO2 and approximately 5 nmol CO2 per minute per mg core protein using their topology and stoichiometry. Malate also incorporates externally supplied acetyl-CoA carbon, and these printed values/uncertainties are not independently reconstructed.

nodes.name: CETCH 1.0 reported incomplete combined turn
nodes.shortDescription: In the source CETCH 1.0 all-components-from-start test, CoA-ester conversion stopped at methylsuccinyl-CoA before a complete cycle turn. This is an explicit reported non-completion result, distinct from unknown assay details and from the authors’ proposed electron-acceptor explanation. The underlying Figure S6 traces and numerical observation window remain unread.

nodes.name: CETCH 1.0 proposed electron-acceptor bottleneck
nodes.shortDescription: The authors interpret the CETCH 1.0 combined-operation stall as a methylsuccinyl-CoA dehydrogenase bottleneck. They propose that, at the usable 0.1 mM ferrocenium level, reduction by NADPH together with slow ferrocene reoxidation most likely prevented effective cycling; higher starting ferrocenium is reported to precipitate other enzymes. This is the source’s mechanism attribution, unresolved by the presently reviewed controls, rather than a newly verified causal identification.

nodes.name: CETCH 1.0 reported stepwise conversion
nodes.shortDescription: The source reports HPLC-MS evidence that successive enzyme additions in CETCH 1.0 convert supplied propionyl-CoA into key pathway intermediates. This establishes source-reported stepwise conversion within the described preparation; it does not establish recurrent operation when all components are present together.

nodes.name: CETCH 5.4 supplied enzyme and resource assembly
nodes.shortDescription: The admitted CETCH 5.4 preparation is an externally assembled enzyme network supplied with propionyl-CoA, labeled bicarbonate and cofactors/regeneration/protection resources. The source reports thirteen core reactions with auxiliary proofreading and cofactor regeneration, catalyzed by seventeen enzymes, plus a malate-synthase/externally supplied acetyl-CoA product trap. This record describes the supplied system and its material boundary; individual resource necessity and an arrangement-only intervention are not established.

nodes.name: DNA-input and RNA-product composition comparison
nodes.shortDescription: The source compared nucleotide composition of RNA synthesized by the purified E. coli fraction with supplied natural DNA or synthetic alternating DNA copolymers. Selected radiolabel/alkaline-degradation methods and the single- versus double-stranded phiX174 DNA comparison test bulk compositional correspondence while retaining strand and sequence limitations.

nodes.name: E. coli enzyme-fraction DNA-dependent RNA incorporation
nodes.shortDescription: The source purified an RNA-synthesizing fraction from E. coli B and assayed labelled ribonucleoside-triphosphate incorporation into acid-insoluble material with supplied DNA, other triphosphates, divalent cations and buffer. Matched component omissions and chemical/RNase/DNase product tests distinguish the selected preparation and its RNA-product interpretation.

nodes.name: Finite chaperone and quality-control source scope
nodes.shortDescription: Resolve original card 3.20 to the selected purified GroEL/SR1/GroES client protocols, retaining finite activity recovery, fluorescence and solution-association observations. Folding assistance and aggregation prevention are supported within those preparations; cellular monitoring, persistent proteome-wide maintenance, damaged-client degradation routing and adaptive stress reliability remain outside admission.

nodes.name: Chaperone activity, proxy and aggregation boundary
nodes.shortDescription: For this review a chaperone intervention is specified by client, components, nucleotide and solution protocol. Enzyme activity recovery, fluorescence, scattering and size-fractionation signals retain separate meanings; aggregation prevention and intrinsic microscopic folding acceleration are different claims. The selected purified assays do not define a universal integrated damage-surveillance/degradation architecture.

nodes.name: Conditional aggregation-prevention account of refolding assistance
nodes.shortDescription: For these Rubisco and DM-MBP preparations the source evidence supports aggregation as a competing solution fate and chaperonin-dependent recovery under the declared protocols. DM-MBP rate equivalence after changing the solution protocol limits a necessary cage-only acceleration account for that comparison. The source passive-cage interpretation remains conditional; no universal identity of microscopic folding paths or absence of active chaperonin effects follows.

nodes.name: Prepared tRNA-osmolyte intervesicle membrane-area competition
nodes.shortDescription: The source compares prepared 2:1 myristoleate:glycerol-monomyristoleate vesicles with supplied tRNA as an internal osmolyte against low-osmolarity vesicles of the same membrane composition. Main text reports tRNA at 83 mg/ml, approximately 0.26 M nucleotide equivalents. Alternate FRET labelling follows relative membrane area in separate comparison arms. Detailed recipe and calibration remain outside the unread Supporting Online Material.

nodes.name: Chromatin assay and causal interpretation boundary
nodes.shortDescription: Distinguish locus bisulfite and histone/factor-associated ChIP, transposase accessibility, population contact profiles, nuclear RNA abundance and protein output. Correlation, broad perturbation, cohort persistence and inherited causal memory are separate claims.

nodes.name: Scoped accessibility, contact and expression profiles
nodes.shortDescription: The reused mouse studies report accessibility, population contact and RNA-profile differences in their own selected preparations. These supply bounded organization/expression associations and perturbation responses, not a unique physical packing geometry or a demonstrated packaging-to-expression causal mechanism.

nodes.name: Scoped accessibility, contact and expression profiles context
nodes.shortDescription: Reuse only the named original assay contexts and complete source limits. Keep bulk/cohort sampling, drug/genetic perturbations, separate molecular profiles and unresolved source discrepancies explicit.

nodes.name: Demixing, mobility and partition boundary
nodes.shortDescription: Distinguish reversible dense/dilute protein demixing, qualitative tracer mobility, labeled-solute partition and fitted interaction models. One supplied Ddx4 terminal-region preparation family does not establish all coacervates, catalytic enhancement, a unique microscopic force, equilibrium criticality or membrane-like transport/gradient control.

nodes.name: Finite Ddx4 condensate scope
nodes.shortDescription: Card 3.18 is qualified to supplied disordered Ddx4 terminal-region reversible demixing, qualitative tracer mobility and labeled-DNA partition in three distinct source preparations. No universal coacervate family, directly resolved fusion or fission mechanism, catalytic/metabolic benefit, measured solvent ordering or first protocellular compartment follows. Original protein-folding, enzyme-catalysis and prior metabolic-compartment necessities are not established.

nodes.name: Cooperativity, sequential binding and site-count boundary
nodes.shortDescription: For this review, binding cooperativity denotes occupancy-dependent binding preference within a declared molecular preparation. A nonlinear curve, a sequential-fit constant, a phenomenological Hill coefficient and a molecular site count have different roles. No Hill coefficient is fitted in the selected CAPN paper, so no Hill value, Hill-to-site-count conversion or Hill-based mechanism assignment is admitted. Its negative-cooperativity interpretation uses the two-site dimer model together with NMR and calorimetry.

nodes.name: Scoped CAPN binding cooperativity
nodes.shortDescription: Card3.5 is qualified to negative sequential cAMP-binding cooperativity in prepared dimeric CAPN, with site-assigned NMR and separate calorimetry. Coupled binding/dynamic behavior is retained without inferring positive amplification, a universal Hill/site-count rule, catalytic turnover or a unique allosteric mechanism.

nodes.name: Ddx4 labeled-DNA partition proxy
nodes.shortDescription: The source background-subtracted confocal images show higher ssDNA-associated signal inside the Ddx4N1 droplets and lower dsDNA-associated signal there relative to surrounding solution. This is a finite fluorescent-solute partition observation under source dye/photophysics and sampling assumptions, not a general DNA-sequence specificity panel, kinetic transport measurement or measured reaction-rate benefit.

nodes.name: Qualitative Ddx4 droplet fluorescence recovery
nodes.shortDescription: The source in vitro Ddx4 droplet fluorescence recovers following photobleaching, supporting mobility of the tracer in that reported preparation. The main/SI mixture annotations and diffusion-model assumptions preclude an independently admitted exact diffusion constant or universal viscosity/exchange mechanism.

nodes.name: Reversible Ddx4 terminal-region demixing
nodes.shortDescription: In source Figure 3D the supplied disordered Ddx4N1 sample develops dense droplets/turbidity during cooling and becomes optically dispersed again upon heating; repeated cycles use the same sample. This supports reversible source-specific demixing with onset/disappearance hysteresis, not a universal concentration threshold or a folded-helicase catalytic mechanism.

nodes.name: Finite DNA-dependent RNA-product synthesis
nodes.shortDescription: The selected E. coli enzyme-fraction assay gives DNA- and divalent-ion-dependent labelled CMP incorporation, strongly reduced by the declared component omissions. The product is alkali-sensitive and largely RNase-sensitive. These results support finite enzyme-fraction-dependent RNA synthesis from supplied inputs, rather than a complete sequence-resolved or physiologically regulated transcription cycle.

nodes.name: Finite heat separation of DNA isotope subunits
nodes.shortDescription: Heating the hybrid-labelled E. coli DNA preparation replaces its intermediate-density band with two separated species comparable to the heated heavy and light references. Together with the source apparent molecular-weight response, this supports physically separable conserved nitrogen-bearing subunits, without direct chemical identification of every subunit or a measured in-vivo separation pathway.

nodes.name: Finite parental-DNA nitrogen partition
nodes.shortDescription: After the heavy-to-light nitrogen shift, intermediate-density DNA accumulates as the initially heavy band declines. Around one population generation the principal band is intermediate; later light and intermediate bands coexist with changing proportions. The source interprets this pattern as equal partition and conservation of parental nitrogen-bearing subunits during DNA duplication, consistent with semiconservative copying under the declared model and preparation.

nodes.name: Finite DNA-dependent RNA composition
nodes.shortDescription: The source reports RNA-product base-composition changes with different supplied DNA preparations and complementary composition for the selected single-stranded DNA input. This supports a finite DNA-dependent compositional constraint on RNA synthesis, without direct sequence fidelity, unique strand choice or complete in-vivo transcription regulation.

nodes.name: Ion electrochemical potential and driven-state bookkeeping
nodes.shortDescription: The ion electrochemical potential includes chemical activity and electric potential: μ̃B = μB° + RT ln aB + zBFφ. Transfer equilibrium requires equal electrochemical potentials. Pump-driven activities, reaction quotients and potentials can change while the intrinsic standard equilibrium constant of the same net reaction at fixed conditions remains unchanged.

nodes.name: Reaction-rate and elementary-step conventions
nodes.shortDescription: Conventions that separate observed concentration change, reaction rate, reaction order and elementary-step molecularity.

nodes.name: Finite enzymatic-complex source scope
nodes.shortDescription: Resolve original card 3.6 to the source-supported synthetic GOx/HRP DNA-cage assembly and coupled product response, retaining labeling, calibration, active-fraction and preparation limits. Assembly and larger activity are finite observations; direct substrate channeling, reduced diffusive loss, synchronized feedback and universal multi-enzyme superiority are excluded from admission.

nodes.name: Scoped enzyme transformation and localized active-site evidence
nodes.shortDescription: Selected KSI mutant assays provide source-fitted reaction turnover and a separate ligand-analogue structure/probe analysis; selected T4 lysozyme experiments provide preparation-dependent glycan products and qualified residue-mechanism interpretations. Together they support finite enzyme transformation and localized active-site functionality while keeping activity, fitted kinetic parameters, structure and mechanistic explanation distinct.

nodes.name: Enzyme assembly, coupled activity and channeling boundary
nodes.shortDescription: Distinguish scaffold assembly/localization, a coupled two-enzyme product signal, intrinsic/active-fraction changes, intermediate retention and direct substrate channeling. Source-specific activity differences between synthetic cage preparations do not make channeling or a universal efficiency gain follow from assembly, and porous cages are not automatically pathway-insulating compartments.

nodes.name: Scoped chromatin-modification and response evidence
nodes.shortDescription: The reused rat study reports locus-specific methylation/chromatin contrasts and broad TSA-associated molecular responses. These support finite environmentally responsive chromatin observations, while causal mediation, general sequence independence and inherited regulatory memory remain unestablished.

nodes.name: Scoped chromatin-modification and response evidence context
nodes.shortDescription: Reuse only the named original assay contexts and complete source limits. Keep bulk/cohort sampling, drug/genetic perturbations, separate molecular profiles and unresolved source discrepancies explicit.

nodes.name: Membrane morphology context
nodes.shortDescription: Source Figure 7 PG-pathway cryo-EM snapshots of pre-existing vesicles: initial material, 1.5 mM oleic-acid addition, subsequent phospholipid-production/stacked states and EDTA-treated material. A second preparation combines lower magnesium with supplied 0.3 mM fatty-acid doses to 1.5 mM total. Exact lower magnesium and some morphological sampling details are unresolved. The two preparations change more than one variable and are not tracked vesicle lineages or the R18 PA sample.

nodes.name: Supplied PA synthesis context
nodes.shortDescription: Source SI Figure S3 PA time course with supplied FadD, PlsB and PlsC in pre-existing liposomes and externally supplied oleic acid, CoA, ATP and glycerol 3-phosphate. The explicit SI procedure uses assay buffer at pH 8 with magnesium, KCl, glycerol and reductant, 2.7 mM oleic acid, 2.67 mM liposomal lipid, 50 micromolar CoA, 5 mM ATP and 1 micromolar PlsB; these are different from the general main PA default. Extracted lipid ion signals are assigned by LC-MS and normalized to DDM. This is a finite three-enzyme PA subsystem, not every eight-enzyme PE/PG assay.

nodes.name: Membrane R18 dye-dilution context
nodes.shortDescription: Source Figure 6 R18 self-quenching assay in pre-existing 2.67 mM DOPC/DOPG/DOPE liposomes with 5 mole percent R18, supplied 2.7 mM oleic acid and the three PA enzymes/resources. Compare the stated spectra before/after fatty-acid addition and PA conversion, with Triton maximal emission normalization. This preparation is separate from SI S3 chemistry and PG cryo-EM; a dye-dilution signal alone is not isolated synthesis-driven bilayer-area growth.

nodes.name: Fatty-acid-associated R18 dequenching
nodes.shortDescription: Source Figure 6 shows R18 fluorescence increasing on addition of oleic acid to pre-existing labeled liposomes; subsequent PA synthesis adds little further fluorescence change. The source uses dye-dilution assumptions to estimate membrane expansion, while the immediate optical response itself does not depend on enzymatic lipid synthesis or uniquely identify increased bilayer surface area.

nodes.name: Reused cGMP rod-patch context
nodes.shortDescription: Reuse the existing inside-out retinal rod outer-segment plasma-membrane patch context and cytoplasmic cGMP application from the primary abstract. The source record leaves species unresolved and admits only reversible cationic conductance change. Full preparation, buffer and temperature are not inferred from other channel studies.

nodes.name: Protein folding, structural inference and functional assay boundary
nodes.shortDescription: Use protein folding here for a specified protein preparation changing its conformational organization. A chemical-group assay, spectrum, restrained structural ensemble, catalytic assay, receptor response and inferred free-energy difference are distinct observables or interpretations. Native denotes a source-assigned functional folded regime under specified conditions; it does not define a unique universal structure or guarantee that every chain reaches it spontaneously.

nodes.name: Reused transducin/PDE biochemical context
nodes.shortDescription: Reuse only the recorded Fung abstract, preparation and two biochemical observables. Preserve the original reading limit and separate molecular activity from electrical response and any larger pathway model.

nodes.name: DNA, RNA and polypeptide readout distinctions
nodes.shortDescription: For these selected studies, a density-band position reports nitrogen-isotope composition under the source buoyant-density assumptions; acid-insoluble nucleotide incorporation with chemical/enzyme tests reports a qualified RNA product; and acid-precipitable amino-acid radioactivity with product tests reports qualified polypeptide synthesis. Bulk isotope or base composition, product solubility and incorporated radioactivity do not by themselves measure complete sequence, copying error frequency, codon length, molecular machine structure or inherited functional continuity.

nodes.name: Source-supported GOx-HRP cage association
nodes.shortDescription: TEM and a native dual-color gel support a DNA cage-associated GOx/HRP population with two nominal enzyme components. Single-enzyme TIRF colocalization yields are high for GOx/HRP in the source calibration, while photobleaching copy estimates depend on labels/detection and are not direct exact stoichiometry of every co-caged pair. This is a prepared synthetic enzyme-scaffold assembly, not a new atom-resolved complex or universal formation stage.

nodes.name: Controlled GOx-HRP cage preparation comparison
nodes.shortDescription: The source compares co-caged, separately full-caged, separately half-caged and uncaged GOx/HRP preparations in the same stated substrate/reporter assay, including free enzyme plus empty-cage and SI thermal/background controls. This is a controlled combined preparation comparison; active fractions and local chemical/physical effects are not individually isolated.

nodes.name: Conditional finite enzyme-compartment account
nodes.shortDescription: The source combination supports a prepared two-enzyme DNA-cage assembly and a larger coupled activity signal under selected conditions. Since separate cages and half-cages also enhance activity, the co-caged advantage is compatible with several local-environment/active-fraction/proximity contributions; it does not uniquely demonstrate an intermediate handoff, retained pathway flux, synchronized feedback or a necessary closed compartment.

nodes.name: Preparation-dependent coupled GOx-HRP activity
nodes.shortDescription: Figure 3 reports approximately8 fold normalized activity for a co-caged GOx/HRP pair relative to the stated uncaged pair plus empty-cage reference; separately full-caged and half-caged preparations give about 4 fold and 3 fold in that comparison. SI Figure 12 shows the associated410 nm absorbance traces and controls. These are source-dependent coupled-signal normalizations, not universal enhancements, exact single-enzyme turnover ratios or direct channeling measurements.

nodes.name: Glutathione-coupled optical redox reporter convention
nodes.shortDescription: Grx1-roGFP2 reports the optical oxidation state of a glutathione-coupled fusion sensor in the sampled cellular region. A fluorescence ratio is not a direct GSH or GSSG concentration, intracellular peroxide concentration, or free NAD redox potential. Converting it to glutathione potential requires the declared sensor-equilibration and reference assumptions.

nodes.name: Purified Grx1-roGFP2 characterization context
nodes.shortDescription: The source compared purified Grx1-roGFP2 with unfused and catalytic-control reporters using optical ratios during defined redox-buffer changes and glutathione-dependent oxidation controls.

nodes.name: Finite glutathione-coupled purified-sensor response
nodes.shortDescription: The active Grx1 fusion responded rapidly to glutathione redox changes in the source comparisons, whereas unfused or catalytic-control reporters responded differently. Peroxide-induced oxidation of the purified fusion depended on glutathione in the tested mixture.

nodes.name: Conditional separation of global RNA folding and catalytic response
nodes.shortDescription: The selected studies support ion- and sequence-dependent RNA conformation and reaction activity in prepared hammerhead complexes. Penedo loop perturbations shift global-FRET titrations and reduce a separate synthetic-RNA cleavage response. Boots finds similar global stem-proximity responses for four divalent ions despite markedly differing apparent reaction rates. Thus a global-folding proxy is insufficient to identify catalytic competence or a unique chemical mechanism; local structure, reactive population and chemistry remain distinct explanations.

nodes.name: Prepared HeLa intracellular reporter context
nodes.shortDescription: The source followed ratiometric fluorescence in Grx1-roGFP2-expressing HeLa cells during an oxidizing challenge, an externally imposed reducing reversal, and separate smaller-challenge time courses; unfused reporter behavior was compared.

nodes.name: HeLa intracellular reporter oxidation and reversal
nodes.shortDescription: The HeLa fusion-sensor ratio rose after the oxidizing challenge and reversed after added reductant. Separate smaller challenges produced shorter-lived ratio deflections that returned toward baseline. These are finite intracellular reporter trajectories, with imposed reversal distinguished from unassisted recovery.

nodes.name: Resolution-limited HEWL conformational comparison
nodes.shortDescription: Superposition with a cited native tetragonal lysozyme structure gives source C-alpha RMS difference0.64 angstrom, comparable to its approximate0.6 angstrom coordinate-error estimate; differences between native crystal forms are also comparable. The source therefore resolves no significant lysozyme tertiary change at this resolution. Unbound D1.3 was unavailable, so the same data do not establish an unchanged antibody interface or select a binding mechanism.

nodes.name: Source-refined HEWL-D1.3 structural model
nodes.shortDescription: The source diffraction/refinement supports a bound HEWL-D1.3 Fab model at 2.8 angstrom, with R=0.28 and estimated coordinate error about 0.6 angstrom. It resolves an extended Fab conformation and a protein-protein interface. Contact geometry is inferred from this resolution-limited model; no new solution trajectory, binding rate or energetic partition is obtained.

nodes.name: Finite HEWL-D1.3 interface geometry
nodes.shortDescription: In the source refined model,16 lysozyme residues and 17 Fab residues contact across a roughly30-by 20 angstrom interface. The contacting lysozyme residues lie within two sequence stretches,18-27 and 116-129, adjacent on the folded surface. All six source-defined CDRs and two adjacent framework residues participate; Table 3 assigns hydrogen-bond-compatible contacts among other close packing. Source calculated buried accessible areas are about 748 square angstrom for lysozyme and 690 for Fab. These counts/areas describe this model and convention, not universal epitope size or energetic contribution.

nodes.name: Hydration relaxation versus structure and ion-distribution boundary
nodes.shortDescription: For the selected source, distinguish measured water-nuclear relaxation, fitted spectral densities, apparent amplitudes/correlation times, model-estimated surface-water numbers and conditional rotation/residence interpretations. These do not directly image spatial ordering or ion distributions. Nonlocal dipolar sampling in NOE theory is not evidence of long-range physical solvent order or a causal effect on binding/catalysis.

nodes.name: Calibrated intracellular-pH reporter convention
nodes.shortDescription: In the selected yeast study, intracellular pH is estimated from the pHluorin excitation ratio using a source standard curve. It is distinct from external-medium pH, proton-pump flux, buffering capacity, membrane potential and concentrations of other ions. Recovery of the reporter-derived pH is an observed trajectory; a particular feedback mechanism is a further interpretation.

nodes.name: Channel conductance versus transport-object boundary
nodes.shortDescription: For the selected abstract, a reversible cGMP-sensitive patch conductance is a finite functional readout. A channel molecular structure, pore geometry/charge, resolved single-channel event, transporter/pump coupling, origin of a membrane boundary and whole-cell ionic-asymmetry maintenance are different claims and are not established by that response alone.

nodes.name: Finite channel and membrane-transport source scope
nodes.shortDescription: Resolve original card 3.3 to the unchanged existing Fesenko abstract-supported conductance finding and its limited patch context. Reversible cGMP-sensitive patch conductance is supported; molecular pore/gating structure, all-channel selectivity/coupled transport, membrane-origin and ionic-maintenance architectures remain outside this evidence scope.

nodes.name: Prepared pKSI Y16S/D40N equilenin crystal
nodes.shortDescription: Crystallize pKSI Y16S/D40N with one equivalent equilenin by hanging-drop mixing of 2 microlitres 30 mg/ml protein stock and 2 microlitres reservoir containing 0.9 M ammonium sulfate and 40 mM potassium phosphate pH 7.2. Grow at 20 C, cryoprotect using sodium malonate and collect 100 K diffraction. Molecular replacement, refinement and a held-out 5% diffraction subset yield deposited model 3IPT.

nodes.name: KSI limits on microscopic catalytic-energy inference
nodes.shortDescription: A bounded interpretation of the admitted KSI variant, analogue-structure and probe records, retaining their separate preparations and solvation assumptions.

nodes.name: Initial-rate kinetic parameters for the selected KSI assay
nodes.shortDescription: For the selected initial-rate fit, v0/[E] = kcat*[S]/(KM+[S]) defines the source Michaelis-Menten parameters. kcat has units s^-1 and KM concentration units; kcat/KM has units M^-1 s^-1. The fit is a response model for this preparation and does not by itself identify microscopic steps or make KM an equilibrium binding constant.

nodes.name: Prepared pKSI variants and 5(10)-EST initial-rate assay
nodes.shortDescription: Compare purified Pseudomonas putida KSI wild type and Y16A, Y16G, Y16S, Y16T and Y16F variants using 5(10)-estrene-3,17-dione at 25 C in 40 mM potassium phosphate pH 7.2, 1 mM EDTA, 2 mM DTT and 2% DMSO. Monitor 248 nm absorbance and fit initial velocity over substrate 2-384 micromolar. The SI reports at least three assays with enzyme concentration varied over at least fourfold; purification/refolding alternatives gave activities agreeing within error.

nodes.name: Localized pKSI analogue-binding geometry
nodes.shortDescription: The source-refined 1.63 angstrom pKSI Y16S/D40N-equilenin structure places Ser16 hydroxyl and equilenin oxygen 6.4 angstrom apart, with Ser16 directed toward Met13 backbone carbonyl. Asp103 remains close to the ligand oxygen. The overall backbone differs by about 0.4 angstrom RMSD from the inherited WT-analogue structure. Local diffuse density is compatible with cavity water, while a direct Ser16-to-ligand hydrogen bond is absent in this refined structure.

nodes.name: KSI-bound phenolate environment-sensitive spectrum
nodes.shortDescription: The source reports 19F peaks at -134.7 ppm for phenolate bound to pKSI Y16F/D40N and -136.4 ppm for Y16S/D40N. The water-to-THF probe comparison shifts by 2.2 ppm. These finite spectra support differing local probe environments and enter the water-filled-cavity interpretation together with diffraction and mutation kinetics.

nodes.name: Prepared KSI fluorophenolate and solvent controls
nodes.shortDescription: Acquire 19F spectra at 20 C for1 mM 2-fluoro-4-nitrophenolate bound to 2 mM pKSI Y16S/D40N or Y16F/D40N in 40 mM potassium phosphate pH 7.2, 1 mM EDTA, 2 mM DTT and 10% D2O, referenced to external trifluoroacetic acid. Compare free probe in water and THF with base. UV-vis confirms bound ligand ionization; labelled-urea refolding/HSQC controls test whether diffuse crystal density is retained urea.

nodes.name: Conditional KSI mutation and solvation interpretation
nodes.shortDescription: Combining the variant turnover losses, Y16S/D40N analogue geometry and fluorophenolate solvent comparisons, Kraut and colleagues propose that smaller residue 16 substitutions allow cavity water to mitigate loss of the Tyr donor, whereas Phe16 adds unfavorable desolvation beyond removing the Tyr hydrogen bond. The measured mutation effects therefore do not directly equal the energetic contribution of one hydrogen bond to catalysis.

nodes.name: Source-fitted pKSI Y16 variant turnover
nodes.shortDescription: For 5(10)-EST under the declared assay, Table S2 reports wild-type kcat=9.9(0.9) s^-1 and KM=19(4) micromolar. Mutant kcat central values are Y16A 4.8x10^-2, Y16G 4.0x10^-2, Y16S 3.8x10^-2, Y16T 5.2x10^-2 and Y16F 5.4x10^-4 s^-1. Printed WT/mutant turnover ratios are 200,250,260,190 and 19,000 respectively. These variant effects concern fitted turnover under one substrate/condition set.

nodes.name: RNA cross-catalytic pair transfer context
nodes.shortDescription: Main-text paired E/E-prime RNA ligation/amplification assay: supplied seed RNA pair and four sequence-specific component substrates, 25 mM MgCl2, EPPS buffer pH 8.5, 42 degrees C. Newly ligated radiolabeled products are separated by denaturing PAGE and product accumulation is fit to logistic growth. Figure 2 includes batch depletion and six successive five-hour incubations with 4 percent carryover into fresh substrate, totaling 30 hours. Only these main-text-defined boundaries are admitted; complete preparative methods, calibration and supplementary controls are unread.

nodes.name: Finite lipid biosynthesis and membrane scope
nodes.shortDescription: Card 3.27 is qualified to externally supplied enzyme-mediated phospholipid production and finite changes of pre-existing liposomes. The source explicitly does not achieve de novo membrane formation with this pathway. Selective permeability, maintained gradients, localized competing metabolism, autonomous growth/division and universal boundary-generation ancestry remain outside admission.

nodes.name: Lipid synthesis and boundary readout boundary
nodes.shortDescription: Distinguish phospholipid chemical conversion, pre-existing membranes, fatty-acid incorporation, dye dequenching, cryo-EM morphology and measured membrane function. Supplied enzymatic lipid synthesis can accompany membrane-material reorganization without showing the origin of a first membrane, selective permeability, stabilized gradients or autonomous division.

nodes.name: Lymphotactin variant-dependent XCR1 and heparin readouts
nodes.shortDescription: WT and the chemokine-fold-stabilized CC3 variant elicit the reported XCR1 calcium response; W55D, whose NMR resembles Ltn40, has no reported agonist response over 50-750 nM. Heparin chromatography and mixed-variant titration distinguish stronger W55D/Ltn40-like interaction from CC3/Ltn10-like interaction. These are assay- and construct-bounded function/structure associations, not proof that a conformation has a unique biochemical function in every environment.

nodes.name: Controlled heparin-dependent lymphotactin signaling change
nodes.shortDescription: Adding heparin shifts WT Trp55 fluorescence toward the Ltn40-like spectrum and suppresses the WT XCR1 calcium response in the source comparison; CC3 fluorescence and signaling resist that effect, and subsequent CC3 addition activates the same cells. The ligand intervention therefore changes the measured functional response in this preparation; a shift of the structural equilibrium is the supported source interpretation.

nodes.name: Condition-dependent lymphotactin spectra and alternative fold inference
nodes.shortDescription: The source reports two WT Ltn NMR signal sets and exchange peaks, with temperature/salt shifting the populations. Its NOE-constrained Ltn40 model is a dimeric four-stranded beta-sheet arrangement distinct from the chemokine-like Ltn10 monomer. This supplies a finite example against a universal single-fold assignment, while atomic contacts and secondary-structure rearrangements remain structural inferences from spectra and restraints.

nodes.name: Nucleotide-specific passive permeation in prepared vesicles
nodes.shortDescription: The source examines nucleotide release from prepared approximately 100 nm fatty-acid-based vesicles in sodium bicine pH 8.5 at 23 C, using gel filtration followed by radioactivity or UV absorbance. Retain 2:1 myristoleate:monomyristolein as the selected preparation and distinguish nucleotide activation state and the presence or absence of magnesium.

nodes.name: Encapsulated modified-DNA primer extension from external activated monomer
nodes.shortDescription: The source preloads and purifies 2:1 myristoleate:monomyristolein vesicles containing a modified DNA primer annealed to a dC15-bearing template. Externally supplied activated amino-guanosine initiates nonenzymatic extension at 4 C in the declared bicine/imidazole medium. Size-exclusion purification separates any exterior primer-template, and denaturing gel electrophoresis reads product length. A POPC preparation provides a separate membrane-composition comparison at 4 C.

nodes.name: Finite fluorescent oligonucleotide retention
nodes.shortDescription: The source incorporates supplied fluorescein-labelled dA10 into prepared amphiphile vesicles, removes exterior oligonucleotide by size-exclusion separation and follows released versus vesicle-associated fluorescence. The stability assay is sodium bicine pH 8.5 at 23 C with a 24-hour observation; Figure S6 reports the same retention result for the tested membrane compositions.

nodes.name: Composition-dependent vesicle ribose permeability
nodes.shortDescription: Compare the source myristoleate-based and other prepared amphiphile vesicles with encapsulated calcein. Ribose addition produces an osmotic volume response recorded by stopped-flow fluorescence at 23 C in POPSO pH 8.2, with the stated EDTA or magnesium alternative. The apparent solute permeability comes from slower volume recovery after initial water efflux; retain membrane composition, vesicle size and sugar-pulse assumptions.

nodes.name: Controlled MBP refolding-protocol comparisons
nodes.shortDescription: The source compares DM-MBP solution and GroEL/GroES/ATP or SR1/GroES/ATP fluorescence recovery within each declared buffer protocol, with concentration-series and wild-type solution controls. Its additional low-chloride comparison changes buffer, ionic composition/concentration and starting denaturant together, so that between-protocol effect cannot be assigned to chloride alone.

nodes.name: DM-MBP fluorescence recovery and solution scattering
nodes.shortDescription: In the chloride-containing protocol Figure 2A gives apparent fluorescence-recovery rates0.03/min in solution,0.25/min with GroEL/GroES/ATP and 0.19/min with SR1/GroES/ATP. DM-MBP solution recovery slows with increasing concentration and scatters light; wild-type controls lack that concentration dependence and substantial scattering. In the changed chloride-deficient protocol Figure 3 shows reduced solution scattering and similar apparent fluorescence rates near 0.1/min for solution and the two chaperonin arms. This is not a direct MBP functional assay.

nodes.name: Heat response of isotope-labelled E. coli DNA
nodes.shortDescription: The source compared heated and unheated E. coli DNA-containing lysates carrying heavy, light or hybrid nitrogen labels. Equilibrium CsCl ultraviolet density profiles after the reported heat treatment were compared with separately heated heavy/light mixtures, while band-width-based apparent molecular-weight interpretations retained the source solvation caveat.

nodes.name: E. coli B nitrogen-isotope transfer and DNA density bands
nodes.shortDescription: The source grew E. coli B with heavy nitrogen and shifted the supplied nitrogen substrates to lighter isotopic composition. DNA-containing lysates collected across estimated population generations were analysed by equilibrium CsCl density-gradient centrifugation, ultraviolet absorption and microdensitometry; heavy, light and mixed reference preparations defined relative band positions.

nodes.name: Finite metabolic-compartment source scope
nodes.shortDescription: Resolve original card 3.17 to enzyme localization and altered coupled activity within the source synthetic porous DNA-cage preparations. Spatial organization can change this assay response, but pathway insulation, intermediate retention, local gradients, crosstalk suppression, parallel metabolism and sustained network regulation are not demonstrated by the chosen data.

nodes.name: Cyclic regeneration and flux boundary
nodes.shortDescription: Distinguish a designed cyclic topology, stepwise conversion, repeated intermediate labeling, coupled product output, stoichiometric accounting and autonomous regulated metabolism. The supplied CETCH network can support finite recurrent operation without reproducing its enzyme catalysts or proving every steady-state/energy/feedback claim.

nodes.name: Finite metabolic-cycle scope
nodes.shortDescription: Card 3.14 is qualified to repeated intermediate transformation/regeneration and product output in an externally assembled and resourced CETCH 5.4 assay. A supplied enzyme cycle does not establish autocatalytic enzyme production, allosteric feedback stabilization, adaptive persistence, universal energy superiority or unbounded operation. Its relationship to the RNA network is conceptual and supplies no measured cross-system causal edge. Source CETCH 1.0 stepwise success and combined non-completion are represented separately, with unknown protocol details retained and the electron-acceptor explanation unresolved.

nodes.name: Model-vesicle observable and inference boundary
nodes.shortDescription: For these model-vesicle records, define membrane assembly/enclosure, solute permeation, polymer retention, template-directed primer extension, supplied-lipid membrane growth, shear-associated fission and competitive membrane-area redistribution as distinct response categories. A source comparison must identify its membrane composition, cargo, medium, timescale, readout and external input before a broader biochemical or population interpretation is made.

nodes.name: Supercooled BPTI water-relaxation context
nodes.shortDescription: The source primary MRD sample is8.3 mM BPTI in water containing52 percent2H and 17 percent17O at pH*5.2, dispersed as aqueous droplets in heptane/nonionic-surfactant emulsion. Longitudinal water relaxation is measured at-10 and-30 C across8-9 field strengths, with 2H frequencies2.5-92 MHz and 17O frequencies2.2-81 MHz; at-30 C only2H is reported because17O sensitivity is inadequate. Same-isotope bulk-water references are recorded at each field/temperature. The source uses inversion recovery, estimates0.5 percent rate uncertainty and 0.1 C temperature accuracy, then fits its spectral-density model and evaluates parameter uncertainty with 1000 Gaussian-noise Monte Carlo datasets at 68.3 percent confidence. Fits exclude the highest-frequency point as described; no new fit is performed here.

nodes.name: Asymmetric MS2 genome reconstruction context
nodes.shortDescription: The source used single-particle cryo-electron-microscopy reconstruction to examine MS2 capsid and internal RNA density, preserving the distinction between symmetry-averaged and asymmetric maps and between density observation and prior-model fitting.

nodes.name: Ordered asymmetric MS2 RNA density
nodes.shortDescription: The source-reported 8.7 angstrom asymmetric MS2 reconstruction contains ordered branched RNA stem-loop density within the protein shell and an uneven distribution of RNA-capsid associations. Much of the density lies near the capsid, with contact assignments concentrated on one side. This is a finite in-situ structural observation, with sequence tracing and pathway interpretation limited by resolution.

nodes.name: Finite MS2 association with isolated pili
nodes.shortDescription: The selected tomographic observations and reconstruction show MS2 particles associated with the sides of isolated bacterial pili. They support a finite phage-receptor structural association without demonstrating a complete genome-delivery event into an intact host.

nodes.name: Isolated MS2-pilus structural context
nodes.shortDescription: The source examined MS2 particles associated with isolated bacterial pili using cryo-electron tomography and averaging of repeated asymmetric particle-receptor complexes, keeping initial association separate from downstream cellular events.

nodes.name: Cell-free MS2 optical assembly context
nodes.shortDescription: The source recorded interferometric optical-intensity time traces from individual surface-associated MS2 RNA/coat-protein assemblies, related the signal to a stated calibration and compared separate electron-microscopy morphology observations.

nodes.name: Finite MS2 optical assembly trajectories
nodes.shortDescription: In the selected cell-free MS2 observations, individual optical traces began after variable delays and then generally increased toward a plateau, with heterogeneous growth patterns and occasional pauses. The source interpreted these finite trajectories as consistent with nucleation followed by growth; separate imaging reported capsid-like and incomplete structures.

nodes.name: Supplied-polyU cell-free phenylalanine incorporation
nodes.shortDescription: The source supplied synthetic polyuridylic acid to a prepared cell-free E. coli W3100 system and measured labelled phenylalanine recovered in acid-precipitable product. Other supplied polynucleotides/uridine compounds and component/inhibitor comparisons bound the response; partial product characterization used extraction, solubility and hydrolysis comparisons with authentic poly-L-phenylalanine.

nodes.name: Nonenzymatic templated extension and replication boundary
nodes.shortDescription: Selected prepared RNA experiments show helper-dependent single additions and finite mixed-monomer chain extension;the unchanged Mansy preparation shows a different externally fed modified-DNA template extension inside vesicles. Together these establish finite nonenzymatic template-guided growth while retaining supplied activation,condition discrepancies and the absence of complete renewable genome replication.

nodes.name: Ddx4 labeled-DNA partition context
nodes.shortDescription: Source Figure 7 and SI Section S8 separate in vitro Ddx4N1 droplet preparation: nominal total protein 162.5 micromolar, 150 mM NaCl after mixing, 1 micromolar total fluorescent 32-base ssDNA or 32-base-paired dsDNA, with a no-DNA fluorescence background. Confocal emission is volume-normalized across ten inside/ten outside regions in each of three fields. Source K is outside/inside. Main paragraph dye annotation differs from caption/method; no exact partition/free-energy or intrinsic binding constant is newly admitted.

nodes.name: Ddx4 qualitative FRAP context
nodes.shortDescription: Source in vitro Figure 3C fluorescent recovery in a roughly 10-micrometer dense Ddx4 droplet at 20 degrees C and nominal 150 mM NaCl. The main text gives Ddx4N1:Ddx4YFP 60:1, whereas SI pages 15-16 list 292.5 micromolar Ddx4N1 plus 8.1 micromolar each Ddx4YFP and free CFP before dilution/hanging-drop equilibration. These composition annotations are unresolved. Use only qualitative fluorescence recovery under the reported preparation, without adopting an exact common mixture or new diffusion coefficient.

nodes.name: Ddx4 thermal demixing context
nodes.shortDescription: Source Figure 3D supplied purified Ddx4N1 N-terminal disordered protein (residues 1-236), 202 micromolar, 200 mM NaCl, pH 8. The same source sample is imaged through cooling from 50 to 22 degrees C and reheating, with repeated cycles. The figure demonstration uses 4 degrees C/min; the separate SI cloud-point sampling defaults to 2 degrees C/min. Retain onset/disappearance hysteresis and operational image/turbidity detection; no universal equilibrium transition is inferred.

nodes.name: Prepared synthetic-RNA hammerhead cleavage assay
nodes.shortDescription: Anneal chemically synthesized hammerhead ribozyme and 32P-labelled substrate strands at pH 7, using a 1000-fold ribozyme excess and a 5-bp stem III. Initiate at 25 C in final 50 mM HEPES pH 7.0, 100 micromolar MgCl2 and 500 mM NaCl. Separate substrate/products by denaturing PAGE with phosphorimaging and fit the fraction-cleaved progress response; compare the internal-loop-complemented substrate under identical conditions.

nodes.name: Finite RNA-catalyzed substrate cleavage under supplied ions
nodes.shortDescription: Penedo reports a fitted apparent cleavage response 0.05 min^-1 for the loop-carrying hammerhead at 100 micromolar MgCl2 plus 500 mM NaCl, pH 7.0 and 25 C. The loop-complemented control shows virtually no cleavage during the 30-min observation. These supplied, chemically synthesized RNA strands show sequence-dependent reaction functionality in the stated mixture.

nodes.name: Prepared noncleavable hammerhead I-III FRET titration
nodes.shortDescription: Assemble Penedo natural-like and loop-disrupted hammerhead constructs from a T7-transcribed long RNA strand and a chemically synthesized fluorescent strand containing deoxy-C17, Cy3 and fluorescein modifications. Purify strands and annealed complexes, record steady-state fluorescence at 4 C, and compare magnesium or sodium concentration titrations using the specified I-III dye vector and two-/three-state response fits.

nodes.name: Loop-dependent hammerhead global FRET transitions
nodes.shortDescription: For the Penedo noncleavable I-III FRET construct, the loop-carrying form shows a magnesium-dependent decrease in FRET described by a two-state concentration fit with midpoint 160 micromolar and Hill coefficient 0.85. The loop-disrupted construct requires two transitions with fitted midpoints 55 micromolar and 2 mM. Sodium produces two resolved titration transitions even in the loop-carrying form; adding moderate sodium to a 100 micromolar magnesium background first reverses and then restores the FRET shift.

nodes.name: Distinct structural, dynamic and lifecycle observables
nodes.shortDescription: Within this review, assembly dynamics, capsid/genome structure, receptor association, maturation, complete cellular entry, productive infection and host-expression reprogramming are distinct observables or hypotheses. Evidence for one does not by definition establish the others.

nodes.name: Preparation-dependent membrane morphology
nodes.shortDescription: Source cryo-EM snapshots show initial vesicles, larger/swollen structures after fatty-acid addition, stacked multilamellar-like material during the high-dose PG pathway and vesicles after EDTA. A distinct lower-magnesium/dosed-feed preparation yields larger vesicles without the displayed stacking. The combined preparation changes do not isolate one causal variable or establish continuous single-vesicle growth, division or membrane barrier function.

nodes.name: Rhodopsin photoisomerization and evidence boundary
nodes.shortDescription: Existing reviewed rhodopsin spectroscopy, wavelength-dependent photolysis and bovine laser-pump structural observations support early light-associated retinal conversion and protein/retinal changes within their separate preparations. Conversion is probabilistic, and the high-fluence structural result retains its multiphoton limit. This is a finite interpretation of original card 3.49, distinct from a folding event, a complete native single-photon mechanism or a later biochemical, electrical or neural response.

nodes.name: Finite polyU-dependent polypeptide synthesis
nodes.shortDescription: Supplied polyU strongly increases labelled-phenylalanine incorporation in the declared cell-free E. coli preparation, whereas the selected alternative polynucleotides/uridine compounds do not replace it. Ribosome/soluble-fraction and energy-system comparisons constrain the preparation. The isolated product has several properties of poly-L-phenylalanine, supporting finite RNA-dependent polypeptide synthesis without a complete codon/frame/fidelity mechanism.

nodes.name: CAPN sequential-binding calorimetry context
nodes.shortDescription: At30C titrate0.6mM cAMP into a30micromolar CAPN preparation using a VP-ITC instrument after dialysis into50mM potassium phosphate pH6.0,500mM KCl and1mM TCEP. Ligand is prepared in the final buffer-exchange flow-through. Discard the preliminary2microliter injection and use the subsequent30 eight-microliter injections. Fit the integrated isotherm using the sequential binding-site model in Origin7.0; NMR preparations use different stated protein concentrations and are not treated as the same physical sample.

nodes.name: CAPN ligand-series NMR and exchange context
nodes.shortDescription: Express and purify His6-tagged CAPN residues1-138 from E. coli CAP, using isotope labeling and nickel/size-exclusion purification as stated. At30C and600MHz record apo, nominal1:1 cAMP:CAPN-dimer and nominal2:1 preparations; the source typically uses0.4mM protein and checks representative relaxation data at0.05,0.4 and1.05mM. Measure backbone chemical shifts, relaxation/dispersion and amide H/D exchange after transfer to D2O. Use the source pD adjustment and identical exchange conditions across ligation states. The complete NMR solution composition and numeric exchange pD are not supplied in the reviewed main-method passages and are not inferred from the separate ITC buffer.

nodes.name: Defined-substrate lysate degradation context
nodes.shortDescription: Engineer N-end-rule-tagged E. coli DHFR/cpLys38, selected C-terminally tagged cpLys38, lysine-less unstructured-tail additions, terminal His6 and linear Ub4 variants as defined in Figures 2-5. cpLys38 joins the old termini with six glycines and starts at former Lys38/ends at Asn37. The N-end-rule construct first carries a cleavable N-terminal ubiquitin followed by a40-residue lac-repressor-derived linker; lysate cleavage exposes the specified Arg or control Met, with ubiquitin-acceptor Lys15/Lys17 or Arg substitutions. Translate35S-labeled substrates in reticulocyte lysate with 12 mM Arg-Ala for N-end-rule substrates, then centrifuge and ammonium-sulfate partially purify. The His6 immunoblot substrate is separately E. coli-expressed and Ni-NTA purified. Resuspend in 25% glycerol,25 mM MgCl2,0.25 M Tris-HCl pH7.4 and dilute five-fold into ATP-depleted rabbit reticulocyte lysate supplemented with 1 mM DTT,5 mM methionine and 25 micromolar ubiquitin. Prewarm25 C for 3 min; initiate with 0.5 mM ATP,10 mM creatine phosphate and 0.1mg/ml creatine phosphokinase. Compare320 micromolar methotrexate with equal-DMSO controls where indicated. Quench time points into SDS-PAGE buffer and quantify radiolabeled full-length/ubiquitinated bands, fragments and, for the separate purified His6 substrate, terminal-epitope immunoblots.

nodes.name: Separate lysate ubiquitination-control context
nodes.shortDescription: Compare N-end-rule Usignal-DHFR and the shortened Usignal-delta15 construct in the same source lysate assay at 25 C, retaining0.5 mM ATP/regeneration and 25 micromolar ubiquitin, but add 2 micromolar Ubal to inhibit deubiquitinating enzymes and 320 micromolar methotrexate to block degradation. Quantify ubiquitinated-band accumulation relative to initial nonubiquitinated radiolabeled substrate by SDS-PAGE/electronic autoradiography. The shortened linker deletes residues 25-40 as described in the source; its delta15 name is retained without silently correcting the source numbering.

nodes.name: Separate cpLys38 global-unfolding control context
nodes.shortDescription: For the Figure 2e control, compare cpLys38 with and without a C-terminal tail at 15 C in 50 mM Tris-Cl pH7.5,0.5 mM EDTA,10 mM KCl,100 micromolar methotrexate and 5 mM MgCl2. Initiate by adding1 micromolar GroEL. At time points withdraw10 microliters into GroEL buffer with 0.1mg/ml proteinaseK,100 micromolar methotrexate and 1 mM DTT at 4 C; after 10 min TCA-precipitate and quantify surviving radiolabeled bands. This control uses a different temperature and methotrexate concentration from degradation.

nodes.name: Prepared nucleotide activation and source boundary
nodes.shortDescription: The Methods report an isolated activated AGC helper preparation with negative-mode ESI/MS m/z996 and spectrophotometric stock concentration. This is a concrete laboratory activated-substrate/intermediate preparation, without a measured universal energy-rich state or autonomous activation supply.

nodes.name: Primitive gradient-to-chemistry coupling remains unresolved
nodes.shortDescription: The catalogue hypothesis that a primitive boundary can couple an electrochemical gradient to internal chemistry remains unestablished by the primary evidence reviewed here. The modern protein-containing Racker preparation does not supply direct evidence for that protein-free primitive coupling claim.

nodes.name: Controlled tag, tail and folded-domain substrate series
nodes.shortDescription: The source deliberately changes N-end-rule tag function, tag-adjacent linker, tail presence/location, cpLys38 versus wild-type DHFR and methotrexate stabilization. The linear G76V Ub4-DHFR fusion supplies a separate targeting design. These constructs define the experimental substrate differences, rather than a natural misfolded/native diagnostic.

nodes.name: Conditional separation of targeting and degradation initiation
nodes.shortDescription: In these folded DHFR model substrates, a source targeting signal can be insufficient for efficient full-length degradation, and an accessible source-assigned unstructured segment can promote engagement and initiate sequential proteolysis at a site separate from tagging. Tag controls, matched ubiquitination and clipping constrain this interpretation. The proposed receptor binding, local unfolding, translocation and release cycle is not observed step-by-step, and substrate sequence/structure can still block complete degradation.

nodes.name: C-terminal clipping without complete stabilized-DHFR destruction
nodes.shortDescription: For wild-type N-Usignal-DHFR-tail-His6 with 320 micromolar methotrexate, the source autoradiogram retains a shorter DHFR-containing product while the terminal His6 immunoblot signal disappears. The source therefore localizes initial clipping to the C-terminal tail. A tail can be removed while a stabilized folded domain persists; disappearance of the terminal tag is not complete client elimination.

nodes.name: Proteasome tagging, initiation and proteolysis boundary
nodes.shortDescription: For these defined substrates, distinguish a ubiquitination signal or engineered Ub4 fusion, ubiquitin-band accumulation, access to a source-assigned unstructured initiation region, conditional unfolding, loss of full-length substrate, terminal clipping and complete degradation. None is interchangeable with universal misfolding recognition, native-protein exclusion or amino-acid recovery.

nodes.name: Ubiquitination control for the shortened N-end-rule linker
nodes.shortDescription: In the separate25 C lysate assay with Ubal and methotrexate, the full Usignal-DHFR and shortened Usignal-delta15-DHFR constructs accumulate ubiquitinated forms at similar source rates and extents. This constrains reduced net ubiquitination as the explanation for slower degradation of the shortened construct, without equating band accumulation to direct proteasome binding.

nodes.name: Source-attributed tail-dependent substrate degradation in lysate
nodes.shortDescription: At25 C, adding a C-terminal lysine-less tail permits degradation of N-end-rule-tagged cpLys38 even with 320 micromolar methotrexate; inactivating the N-end residue, replacing acceptor Lys15/Lys17 or deleting the N-tag strongly inhibits it. Shortening the Usignal linker slows DHFR degradation, while either tested C-terminal tail restores faster band loss. Linear Ub4-DHFR without a tail is degraded inefficiently; tail addition accelerates loss. This is a finite tag-and-initiation-region requirement under the lysate protocol, not an all-substrate rule.

nodes.name: Tail and cpLys38 global-unfolding control
nodes.shortDescription: The Figure 2e GroEL-binding/protease-protection traces for cpLys38 with and without the C-terminal tail are similar at 15 C with 100 micromolar methotrexate. This source control argues against simple global destabilization as the sole explanation under its own conditions. It does not establish equal local unfolding or a measured unfolding rate during the25 C degradation assay.

nodes.name: Scoped distal CAPN allosteric response
nodes.shortDescription: Card3.12 is qualified to controlled cAMP-dependent changes in remote CAPN relaxation and exchange readouts, combined with source-inferred binding preference. The finite result supports distal regulation within the prepared assembly while leaving microscopic communication, structural exclusivity and biological function outside the selected measurements.

nodes.name: Scoped folding, functional readout and kinetic-stability evidence
nodes.shortDescription: Card 3.0 is qualified to prepared RNase recovery of catalytic/physical readouts, lymphotactin condition-dependent alternative folds with construct-bounded functional assays, and an alpha-lytic-protease kinetic-metastability inference. These cases connect sequence-bearing molecular preparations, conformation-sensitive observations and specified activities.
